---

->QUESTION CXII<-

ON BOASTING <note>original: "De Jactantia"</note>. — Divided into two articles.

Afterwards we must consider boasting and irony <note>meaning self-deprecation or understatement</note>, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 7.
First, regarding boasting, two things are asked: 1. to which virtue it is opposed; 2. whether it is a mortal sin.

->FIRST ARTICLE<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, the procedure is as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes there can be boasting even without lying; as when someone displays his own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast..., that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom, and the magnitude and excellence of his power.* Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory in the 23rd book of the *Morals*, chapter 4, near the beginning, as one of the four species of pride, namely when someone boasts of having what he does not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard of the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that his strength is not according to it.* And in the 31st book of the *Morals*, chapter 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ARTICLE I. — Boasting properly so-called is a vice by which someone externally carries himself above what is actually in him. Although boasting, according to the use of the word, is also spoken of regarding the display of the truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others, yet as a vice in its own kind (for thus only is it properly taken), it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; since only in this way is it the name of a vice in its own kind. For the display of the truth beyond the knowledge of others is not evil in its own kind, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil because of an evil end (Cajetan).</margin>

(1) The Vulgate: ... The riches of the glory of his kingdom.

<column-break/>

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by riches; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What hath pride profited us, or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of riches seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— On the contrary, is what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the second and fourth books of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, in both places, that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that it must be said that boasting properly seems to imply that a man extols himself in words. For those things which a man wishes to throw <term>jactare</term> <gloss>to throw or boast</gloss> far, he lifts up high. Now a man properly extols himself when he says something about himself that is above himself. This indeed happens in two ways: — for sometimes someone speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in him, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle <note>Paul</note>, recoiling from, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or anything he heareth from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in him according to the truth of the matter. And because a man is to be judged more according to what is in himself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it follows that it is more properly called boasting when someone carries himself above what is in him than when he carries himself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting properly so-called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds from boasting according to how it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body of the article and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which it happens, if not always, yet more frequently, and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an internal motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is inwardly lifted up above himself through arrogance, it usually follows that externally he boasts of certain greater things about himself, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and delights in this, because such is his habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is extolled above himself, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is more frequently its cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, a boaster usually aims at achieving glory through his boasting; and therefore according to Gregory it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

(1) In the Nicholas edition the word "utrobique" <gloss>in both places</gloss> is missing.

<summary>Aquinas defines boasting as a vice of excess opposed to the virtue of truth, distinguishing between boasting that exceeds public opinion and boasting that exceeds the actual truth of one's character.</summary>
